---
title: "Figures"
---

## One set of tables, three ways to draw them

All three backends read their numbers from the same place, `qdapy.frames`.
Swapping one for another therefore changes how a figure looks and never what it
says, which also means you can start in seaborn and move to plotnine halfway
through a paper without re-checking the values.

Everything on this page is *live*: the code is executed when the
documentation is built, and the figures are its actual output. The material
is [the example study](example-data.qmd) that ships with the package — a
synthetic study on workload in nursing, nine codes in three themes, eight
interviews from two settings, coded by two people:

```{python}
import qdapy

frag = qdapy.read_fragments(qdapy.example("zotqda-fragments-demo.csv"))
```

The correspondence analysis puts codes **and** interviews into one map, and
carries its own caveat: the share of inertia the two dimensions show is
printed inside the figure, because a map without it looks equally
trustworthy at 30% and at 90%:

```{python}
#| label: fig-ca
#| fig-cap: "Codes and documents in one correspondence-analysis map. The two settings separate along dimension 1, each surrounded by the codes typical for it — and the figure itself states how much of the structure it shows."
qdapy.gg.ca_map(frag)
```

Which codes appear on the same passages? The dendrogram clusters codes by
co-occurrence and prints the cophenetic correlation — how faithfully the
tree preserves the distances — in its title:

```{python}
#| label: fig-dendro
#| fig-cap: "Codes clustered by co-occurrence (Jaccard distance, seaborn backend). The burden/coping pairs built into the material come back out as clusters."
qdapy.sns.dendrogram(frag)
```

And the code-by-document matrix shows the same structure as a heatmap, one
glance telling you which interviews carry which themes:

```{python}
#| label: fig-matrix
#| fig-cap: "Codings per code and interview. The block structure between the two settings is the group difference the map above projects."
qdapy.gg.code_matrix(frag)
```

| Backend | Import | Returns | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| plotnine | `qdapy.gg` | a `ggplot` object | you think in the grammar of graphics, or want the figure to match the R package |
| seaborn | `qdapy.sns` | a matplotlib `Axes` | the figure has to sit inside a layout you already have |
| Vega-Lite | `qdapy.vega` | an Altair chart | the figure has to look exactly like it did in Zotero |

Function names line up across the backends: `frequencies`, `code_matrix`,
`timeline`, `saturation`, `mds`, `level_agreement`, `ca_map`, plus the
`dendrogram` that only `qdapy.sns` provides.

## Nothing appears on its own

No function here calls `plt.show()`. Figures appear when your script says so:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
qdapy.sns.frequencies(frag, ax=left)
qdapy.sns.saturation(history, ax=right)
fig.savefig("figure-2.pdf")
```

Because every seaborn function accepts `ax=`, one of these figures can sit as
a single panel inside a layout that is otherwise entirely yours.

## Reading the numbers off a figure

Often it is the table you want rather than the picture, whether for a
supplement or because a reviewer asked to see the counts. The same calls
that feed the figures return them directly:

```{python}
qdapy.code_counts(frag)
```

```python
qdapy.code_matrix(frag, long=False)   # codes x documents
qdapy.timeline(history)               # cumulative codings per coder
qdapy.saturation(history)             # distinct codes over time
qdapy.mds_points(frag)                # the scaling map as points
qdapy.ca_points(frag)                 # codes and documents in one map
```

The last two are what the map figures are drawn from, and they carry the
number the caption needs in `df.attrs`: `goodness` for the scaling,
`inertia_shown` for the correspondence analysis.

One thing to know about `timeline()`: it counts `add` events and ignores
`remove`. A coding somebody applied and then withdrew did happen, but it is not
part of what you ended up with, and a growth curve that keeps counting it
flatters the result.

## The plugin's own charts

Every chart in qdaZ can be saved as a data-plus-specification pair. Rendering
the specification reproduces the figure exactly as it looked in Zotero:

```python
spec = qdapy.vega.read_spec("frequencies.json")
chart = qdapy.vega.render(spec, qdapy.code_counts(frag))
```

This needs Altair — `pip install "qdaPy[vega]"`. Use it when a figure must
match the plugin; use the other two backends when it must match the rest of
your manuscript.
